Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Orthodontic tooth movement

Several trials report faster movement, including a recent split-mouth study, but this effect is not uniform across protocols or outcomes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several trials report faster movement, including a recent split-mouth study, but this effect is not uniform across protocols or outcomes.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact orthodontic tooth-movement category contains 160 unique titles. The database labels 65 human publications as randomized trials, 11 as other human or case reports, 41 as animal studies, 39 as reviews or syntheses, three as in-vitro or ex-vivo, one as a protocol, and three as editorials or commentaries. Some records carry overlapping methods, and reviews summarize the primary trials. (Balakrishnan et al. 2026)

Human and clinical evidence

Human trials examine movement rate in different teeth and orthodontic stages. Balakrishnan et al. randomized 33 women in a split-mouth design and reported greater canine retraction with LLLT than control over 12 weeks. An earlier randomized study of 34 patients also reported increased molar uprighting movement. Results across studies are mixed, and findings in one tooth or movement task do not establish a general reduction in treatment time. (Ma et al. 2023)

Animal evidence

The database includes 41 animal-tagged titles, predominantly rat studies, with rabbit, dog, and guinea-pig records also present. Animal experiments assess bone remodeling and molecular responses but cannot determine the clinical magnitude or safety of accelerated tooth movement in people.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Three records carry in-vitro or ex-vivo tags. These laboratory findings are separate from clinical tooth-movement outcomes and may overlap reports with animal methods.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols vary in wavelength, dose, point placement, and frequency. The 2026 trial used 650 nm visible red light, 8 J/cm² and a 100 mW diode laser at baseline and weeks four and eight. A separate clinical trial used 808 nm near-infrared light at 25 J/cm². These settings illustrate variation rather than a validated optimum.

Interpretation

The literature suggests that PBM can affect movement in some settings, but study heterogeneity and overlapping reviews limit a general conclusion. Future trials should register protocols, report tooth-specific movement and anchorage outcomes, standardize dosimetry, and assess root resorption, pulp vitality, and final treatment duration.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for tooth-movement acceleration. Many trials report outcome-specific increases, but results vary across dosimetry, tooth movement, and study design.
Publications and records160 unique titles in Oral > Orthodontics > Tooth movement; there is no duplicate title in the 160 database rows.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains 160 unique titles, including many randomized human reports, animal studies, and reviews. Trial protocols, tooth types, schedules, and movement measures differ, and reviews overlap primary reports. Further research should use prespecified movement measures, sham control, and longer-term safety outcomes.
